t: Merge BSTs to Create Single BST: Hash-Guided Leaf Grafting with Validation
o:
**Understanding the problem**

We hold up to 5*10^4 tiny BSTs (at most 3 nodes, no grandchildren, all root values distinct) and may repeatedly graft one tree onto another whenever a leaf value equals the other tree's root value; the leaf is replaced by that root. After exactly n-1 operations everything must form one valid BST whose root we return, or null. In Example 1, [2,1] grafts onto leaf 2 of [3,2,5] and [5,4] grafts onto leaf 5, producing [3,2,5,1,null,4]. In Example 2 grafting [3,2,6] under 5 places 6 inside 5's left subtree, violating BST order, so the answer is null. Example 3 offers no leaf/root match at all. The crux is finding which tree is the final root, attaching every other tree exactly once, and proving the result obeys strict BST ordering.
k: The final root is the unique tree whose root value never appears as anyone's child value; zero or multiple candidates means null.
Graft by copying the subtree's children onto the matching leaf — the leaf keeps its own value (equal to the grafted root), so values stay consistent while the node count shrinks by one per merge.
A strict inorder sweep plus a node-count check catches both wrong placements and stray duplicate leaves that never got merged.

a.i: Simulate the process directly. Identify the unique candidate root, then keep scanning pending trees: whenever some leaf of the growing tree equals a pending tree's root value, attach it and restart the scan since the tree changed. Each attachment does a full-tree leaf search, so this degrades quadratically but follows the operation definition literally.
s: Collect all child values; the tree whose root value is absent from that set is the only possible final root (require exactly one).
While pending trees remain, search the current tree for a leaf equal to some pending root and attach that tree's children there.
Restart after each successful merge; if a full pass merges nothing, stop.
Return null if any tree remains unmerged.
Validate with an iterative inorder traversal requiring strictly increasing values.
a.t: O(n^2 * V) worst case — each of up to n restarts performs an O(V) whole-tree search, where V <= 3n total nodes.
a.sp: O(n) — the pending list plus traversal stacks.

a.n: Approach 2: Hash Map Guided Attachment + Full Validation (optimal)
a.i: Index unmerged trees by root value so the matching leaf can consume its counterpart in O(1): when walking the assembled structure, any leaf whose value sits in the map adopts that tree's children immediately and the entry is removed. After one pass, leftover map entries prove failure. Finally verify the result twice over: an iterative inorder sweep must be strictly increasing (rejecting Example 2), and the visited node count must equal total input nodes minus n-1 discarded roots (rejecting duplicate leaves that silently stayed put).
s: Build value-to-root map and child-value set; require exactly one root candidate.
Walk the growing tree with an explicit stack; whenever a child's value maps to an unmerged tree, splice in that tree's children and delete the map entry.
Fail if any unmerged trees remain.
Run iterative inorder validation demanding strictly increasing values and counting nodes.
Return the root only if the count equals totalNodes - (n - 1).
a.t: O(n) — each of the O(n) nodes enters/leaves stacks a constant number of times thanks to O(1) map lookups.
a.sp: O(n) — hash maps and traversal stacks.

w: Lead with Approach 2; describe the brute force only to motivate the hash map. Pitfalls: assuming the first array element is the root (it almost never is), validating only the shape without the inorder/count checks (Example 2 passes naive structural checks), and discarding the grafted leaf instead of letting it adopt children — the leaf already holds the right value. Remember the answer is null both when merging is impossible and when the merged tree violates BST order. Follow-ups: report the sequence of operations performed (record parent pointers during splicing) or handle trees larger than three nodes (the same algorithm works unchanged).
